parakeet: Christianity did not invent this logic. It later inhabited it. Even more significant is the rise of Sol Invictus, whose prominence peaks in the third century. While solar worship had existed in Rome long before, it was the Emperor Arulian who formally elevated Sol Invictus as an imperial symbol and established December 25th as Dis Nautilus Solus Invicti, the birthday of the unconquered Sun. This was not folk religion, it was imperial theology. Sol Invictus symbolized cosmic stability after political crisis, reinforced unity across a fractured empire, and positioned imperial authority as aligned with universal order. December 25th was chosen because it fell just after the winter solstice when the days begin to lengthen. It was not astronomically precise, but it was symbolically perfect. Darkness does not win, light returns, order is restored, the cosmos is reliable. That narrative proved politically powerful in times of instability and later theologically useful to Christianity. Christianity did not simply need a date for Jesus' birth. It needed a date that could carry hope without eminence, anchor meaning in cyclical time, and feel cosmically inevitable rather than historically fragile. Late December already accomplished this. It framed light overcoming darkness, tied renewal to cosmic rhythm, and allowed rebirth to be celebrated without requiring verification. The calendar did the work the clock could no longer do.
